claim: The twin-arginine translocase (Tat) transports folded proteins across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane.
source: The twin-arginine translocase (Tat) transports folded proteins across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane and the plant thylakoid membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: The twin-arginine translocase (Tat) transports folded proteins across the plant thylakoid membrane.
source: The twin-arginine translocase (Tat) transports folded proteins across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane and the plant thylakoid membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: The Tat translocation site is formed by substrate-triggered oligomerization of the protein TatA.
source: The Tat translocation site is formed by substrate-triggered oligomerization of the protein TatA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Walther and co-workers have proposed a structural model for the TatA oligomer in which TatA monomers self-assemble using electrostatic 'charge zippers'.
source: Walther and co-workers have proposed a structural model for the TatA oligomer in which TatA monomers self-assemble using electrostatic 'charge zippers' (Cell (2013) 132: 15945).
evidence: This references a prior publication by Walther and co-workers.

claim: The charge zipper model was supported by in vitro analysis of the oligomeric state of TatA variants containing charge-inverting substitutions.
source: This model was supported by in vitro analysis of the oligomeric state of TatA variants containing charge-inverting substitutions.
evidence: This references prior work by Walther and co-workers.

claim: Live cell assays of TatA assembly and function in Escherichia coli do not support the charge zipper model.
source: Here we have used live cell assays of TatA assembly and function in Escherichia coli to re-assess the roles of the charged residues of TatA. Our results do not support the charge zipper model.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Substitutions of charged residues located in the TatA amphipathic helix lock TatA in an assembled state.
source: Instead, we observe that substitutions of charged residues located in the TatA amphipathic helix lock TatA in an assembled state, suggesting that these charged residues play a critical role in the protein translocation step that follows TatA assembly.
evidence: This is based on the fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Charged residues in the TatA amphipathic helix play a critical role in the protein translocation step that follows TatA assembly.
source: Instead, we observe that substitutions of charged residues located in the TatA amphipathic helix lock TatA in an assembled state, suggesting that these charged residues play a critical role in the protein translocation step that follows TatA assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that substitutions lock TatA in an assembled state.

claim: The Tat system is found in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane.
source: The Tat protein translocase is found in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, plant thylakoid membrane, and the inner membrane of some mitochondria (Carrie et al., 2016; Celedon and Cline, 2013; Palmer and Berks, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Tat system is found in the plant thylakoid membrane.
source: The Tat protein translocase is found in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, plant thylakoid membrane, and the inner membrane of some mitochondria (Carrie et al., 2016; Celedon and Cline, 2013; Palmer and Berks, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Tat system is found in the inner membrane of some mitochondria.
source: The Tat protein translocase is found in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, plant thylakoid membrane, and the inner membrane of some mitochondria (Carrie et al., 2016; Celedon and Cline, 2013; Palmer and Berks, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The well-studied Tat system of Escherichia coli requires the three membrane proteins TatA, TatB and TatC.
source: The well-studied Tat system of Escherichia coli requires the three membrane proteins TatA, TatB and TatC (Berks, 2015; Cline, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Binding of substrate proteins to a TatBC receptor complex triggers the proton-motive force (PMF)-dependent oligomerization of TatA protomers from a membrane pool onto the substrate-TatBC complex.
source: Binding of substrate proteins to a TatBC receptor complex triggers the proton-motive force (PMF)-dependent oligomerization of TatA protomers from a membrane pool onto the substrate-TatBC complex (Alcock et al., 2013; Dabney-Smith et al., 2006; Rose et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The assembled TatA oligomer promotes translocation of the substrate protein across the membrane.
source: The assembled TatA oligomer promotes translocation of the substrate protein across the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: A single TatA molecule comprises an N-terminal transmembrane helix (TMH), a basic amphipathic helix (APH) lying at the membrane surface, and a natively unstructured tail termed the densely charged region (DCR).
source: A single TatA molecule comprises an N-terminal transmembrane helix (TMH), a basic amphipathic helix (APH) lying at the membrane surface, and a natively unstructured tail termed the densely charged region (DCR) (Figure 1A,B) (Hu et al., 2010; Rodriguez et al., 2013; Walther et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The APH and DCR of TatA molecules have complementary charge patterns.
source: This model arises from the observation that the APH and DCR of TatA molecules have complementary charge patterns (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Salt bridge formation between oppositely charged residues in the APH and DCR was proposed to mediate folding and oligomerisation of TatA.
source: Salt bridge formation between some of these oppositely charged residues was proposed to mediate folding and oligomerisation of TatA resulting in a transport pore as shown in Figure 1C,D.
evidence: This describes the charge zipper model proposed by Walther and co-workers.

claim: Single charge inversion substitutions in B. subtilis TatAd were reported to impede TatA oligomerization.
source: Single charge inversion substitutions were reported to impede TatA oligomerization.
evidence: This references prior work by Walther and co-workers.

claim: For four of the seven predicted salt bridges in B. subtilis TatAd, TatA assembly could be restored by simultaneously inverting the charge on the predicted partner residue.
source: Crucially, for four of the seven predicted salt bridges, they reported that TatA assembly could be restored by simultaneously inverting the charge on the predicted partner residue, thereby re-establishing a salt bridge.
evidence: This references prior work by Walther and co-workers.

claim: TatA complexes can be observed in detergent extracts in the absence of substrate proteins, or the TatBC complex, or the PMF.
source: Whether TatA complexes observed in detergent solution can be directly related to physiological TatA oligomers remains a matter of debate since TatA complexes can be observed in detergent extracts in the absence of substrate proteins, or the TatBC complex, or the PMF, all of which are required for formation of native TatA oligomers (Gohlke et al., 2005; Palmer and Berks, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Substrate proteins, the TatBC complex, and the PMF are all required for formation of native TatA oligomers.
source: Whether TatA complexes observed in detergent solution can be directly related to physiological TatA oligomers remains a matter of debate since TatA complexes can be observed in detergent extracts in the absence of substrate proteins, or the TatBC complex, or the PMF, all of which are required for formation of native TatA oligomers (Gohlke et al., 2005; Palmer and Berks, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The oligomeric states of TatA observed in detergent solution are influenced by the detergent to protein ratio.
source: In addition, the oligomeric states of TatA observed in detergent solution are known to be influenced by the detergent to protein ratio (Cline and Mori, 2001; Rodriguez et al., 2013) casting doubt on whether detergent extraction accurately captures the TatA oligomeric state present in the membrane before solubilization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The first 50 residues of TatA are functionally essential.
source: We examined the four potential salt bridge pairs where both partners are in the functionally essential first 50 residues of TatA (Lee et al., 2002; Warren et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A D31K variant of TatA was unable to export CueO.
source: However, while a D31K variant was unable to export CueO or grow on TMAO, as anticipated if D31 is part of a zipper bridge, a K49D substitution still permitted significant transport of CueO and close to wild-type growth on TMAO (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A D31K variant of TatA was unable to grow on TMAO.
source: However, while a D31K variant was unable to export CueO or grow on TMAO, as anticipated if D31 is part of a zipper bridge, a K49D substitution still permitted significant transport of CueO and close to wild-type growth on TMAO (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A K49D substitution in TatA permitted significant transport of CueO.
source: However, while a D31K variant was unable to export CueO or grow on TMAO, as anticipated if D31 is part of a zipper bridge, a K49D substitution still permitted significant transport of CueO and close to wild-type growth on TMAO (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A K49D substitution in TatA permitted close to wild-type growth on TMAO.
source: However, while a D31K variant was unable to export CueO or grow on TMAO, as anticipated if D31 is part of a zipper bridge, a K49D substitution still permitted significant transport of CueO and close to wild-type growth on TMAO (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Combining the K49D substitution with the D31K substitution failed to restore export of CueO.
source: However, combining the K49D substitution with the inactivating D31K substitution failed to restore export of CueO or growth on TMAO (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Combining the K49D substitution with the D31K substitution failed to restore growth on TMAO.
source: However, combining the K49D substitution with the inactivating D31K substitution failed to restore export of CueO or growth on TMAO (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The D31K/K49D variant exhibited poorer growth on SDS than D31K alone.
source: Nevertheless, the D31K/K49D variant, rather than restoring wild-type Tat transport activity to D31K as predicted by the charge zipper model, exhibited even poorer growth (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A K52D substitution in TatA had only a moderate effect on Tat transport.
source: However, we found that, as with K49D, a K52D substitution had only a moderate effect on Tat transport and did not restore activity to the D31K variant (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: A K52D substitution did not restore activity to the D31K variant.
source: However, we found that, as with K49D, a K52D substitution had only a moderate effect on Tat transport and did not restore activity to the D31K variant (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The acidic D45D46E47 motif is implicated in Tat function.
source: We next examined the consequence of simultaneously removing the three potential salt bridges formed by the acidic D45D46E47 motif (Figure 1A,C), which is already implicated in Tat function (Fröbel et al., 2011; Greene et al., 2007; Hicks et al., 2005; Warren et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disrupting the three salt bridge pairs on the APH side (EDD variant) abolished activity in CueO export and TMAO growth assays.
source: Disrupting these three salt bridge pairs on the APH side (EDD variant) or the DCR side (KKK variant) abolished activity in our CueO export and TMAO growth assays (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Disrupting the three salt bridge pairs on the DCR side (KKK variant) abolished activity in CueO export and TMAO growth assays.
source: Disrupting these three salt bridge pairs on the APH side (EDD variant) or the DCR side (KKK variant) abolished activity in our CueO export and TMAO growth assays (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: A TatA EDD/KKK variant failed to restore detectable activity in CueO export and TMAO growth assays.
source: Nevertheless, a TatA EDD/KKK variant, which inverts the potential salt bridges, failed to restore detectable activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: TatA EDD exhibited a low level of Tat transport activity in the SDS assay that was greater than the negative control.
source: Using the more sensitive SDS assay, TatA EDD exhibited a low level of Tat transport activity that was clearly greater than the negative control (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Restoration of the predicted charge pairs in TatA EDD/KKK completely abolished Tat transport.
source: However, restoration of the predicted charge pairs in TatA EDD/KKK completely abolished Tat transport instead of recovering activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Each TatA variant analysed was present in the membrane at a comparable level to the wild-type TatA protein.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed that each variant analysed was present in the membrane at a comparable level to the wild-type TatA protein (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In resting cells the TatA-YFP fusion is present in the dispersed state, visualised as a halo of fluorescence.
source: In resting cells the TatA-YFP fusion is present in the dispersed state, visualised as a halo of fluorescence (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Overproduction of the Tat substrate CueO drives assembly of TatA-YFP oligomers which appear as bright, mobile fluorescent spots.
source: Overproduction of the Tat substrate CueO drives assembly of TatA-YFP oligomers which appear as bright, mobile fluorescent spots.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: If the proton motive force (PMF) is abolished by addition of CCCP, the TatA oligomers dissociate and fluorescence reverts to the peripheral halo.
source: If the proton motive force (PMF) is abolished by addition of the protonophore carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenyl hydrazone (CCCP), the TatA oligomers dissociate and fluorescence reverts to the peripheral halo.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: All charge zipper variants were able to assemble into fluorescent foci.
source: We found that all our charge zipper variants were able to assemble into fluorescent foci (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Charge zipper substitutions K49D and K52D that retained significant Tat activity fully replicated the TatA-YFP oligomerization behaviour of the wild-type protein.
source: While those charge zipper substitutions that retained significant Tat activity (K49D and K52D) fully replicated the TatA-YFP oligomerization behaviour of the wild-type protein, those charge zipper variants which had very low transport activity (D31K and KKK) remained in the assembled state in all conditions tested.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Charge zipper variants with very low transport activity (D31K and KKK) remained in the assembled state in all conditions tested.
source: While those charge zipper substitutions that retained significant Tat activity (K49D and K52D) fully replicated the TatA-YFP oligomerization behaviour of the wild-type protein, those charge zipper variants which had very low transport activity (D31K and KKK) remained in the assembled state in all conditions tested.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Wild type TatA-YFP protein exhibits perturbed behaviour in strains lacking TatE, being visualised in the assembled state even in the absence of overproduced substrate or the presence of CCCP.
source: Under these conditions it is well-established that the wild type TatA-YFP protein exhibits perturbed behaviour, being visualised in the assembled state even in the absence of overproduced substrate or the presence of CCCP (Alcock et al., 2013; Leake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both high and low activity charge zipper variants were able to form TatA-YFP oligomers in the absence of TatE.
source: We found that both high and low activity charge zipper variants were still able to form TatA-YFP oligomers in the absence of TatE (Figure 3), which eliminates the possibility that TatE was mediating the TatA assembly observed for these variants.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Oligomer formation by charge zipper variants was strictly dependent on the presence of TatBC.
source: Importantly, oligomer formation by these TatA-YFP variants was in all cases strictly dependent on the presence of TatBC (Figure 3) showing that the charge zipper variants still assemble TatA via the physiological route, most likely triggered by endogenous substrates (Alcock et al., 2013), rather than through self-aggregation.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The charge zipper variants still assemble TatA via the physiological route, most likely triggered by endogenous substrates, rather than through self-aggregation.
source: Importantly, oligomer formation by these TatA-YFP variants was in all cases strictly dependent on the presence of TatBC (Figure 3) showing that the charge zipper variants still assemble TatA via the physiological route, most likely triggered by endogenous substrates (Alcock et al., 2013), rather than through self-aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the TatBC-dependence of oligomer formation and supported by citation.

claim: TatA-YFP EDD variant forms TatBC-dependent TatA-YFP assemblies in both the presence and absence of TatE.
source: Although problems with expression level and proteolytic release of YFP meant the TatA-YFP EDD variant could not be directly compared to the other charge zipper variants, it also appears to form TatBC-dependent TatA-YFP assemblies in both the presence and absence of TatE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the charge zipper substitutions prevented TatA oligomerization in live cells.
source: Firstly, and most fundamentally, Walther and co-workers report that charge zipper substitutions affect TatA oligomerization. We found that none of our charge zipper substitutions prevented TatA oligomerization in live cells, even though the majority of our variants were confirmed to have severe functional defects.
evidence: This is based on the fluorescence microscopy data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The majority of charge zipper variants were confirmed to have severe functional defects.
source: We found that none of our charge zipper substitutions prevented TatA oligomerization in live cells, even though the majority of our variants were confirmed to have severe functional defects.
evidence: This is based on the transport assay data presented in Figure 2.

claim: For some of the putative salt bridge variants tested (D31K versus K49D or K52D), there are large differences in transport and oligomerization behavior between substitutions at each end of the salt bridge.
source: Finally, ablation of either end of a predicted charge zipper salt bridge should give rise to the same structural and functional defects. Yet for some of the putative salt bridge variants tested (D31K versus K49D or K52D) we see large differences in transport and oligomerization behavior between substitutions at each end of the salt bridge.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Substitution of the highly conserved and functionally essential APH residue Phe39 results in TatA oligomers that are resistant to loss of the PMF and form even without substrate overproduction.
source: The same behavior has previously been reported following substitution of the highly conserved and functionally essential APH residue Phe39 (Alcock et al., 2013; Hicks et al., 2003; Hicks et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several substitutions in the APH lead to the accumulation of TatA in a stable oligomeric state.
source: Thus, several substitutions in the APH lead to the accumulation of TatA in a stable oligomeric state.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that multiple APH substitutions result in stable TatA oligomers.

claim: The observed TatA oligomerization is not spontaneous, but triggered by endogenous Tat substrates.
source: In each case the observed TatA oligomerization is not spontaneous, but triggered by endogenous Tat substrates, as demonstrated by the dependence on TatBC (Figure 3, (Alcock et al., 2013)).
evidence: This is based on the TatBC-dependence shown in Figure 3 and supported by citation.

claim: The APH is required for a step in the transport cycle between TatA oligomerization and TatA disassembly.
source: The subsequent accumulation of stably assembled TatA oligomers is most parsimoniously explained by suggesting that the APH is required for a step in the transport cycle between TatA oligomerization and TatA disassembly, and that this step is disrupted in the APH variants.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that APH variants form stable oligomers.

claim: The mechanistic step disrupted in APH variants is likely to be the physical movement of the substrate protein across the membrane bilayer.
source: Logically, this mechanistic step is likely to be the physical movement of the substrate protein across the membrane bilayer.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the inference about the APH's role.

claim: Tat null strains have a defective cell envelope that renders them sensitive to SDS.
source: Third, we analysed cell growth on SDS-containing medium because Tat null strains have a defective cell envelope that renders them sensitive to SDS (Stanley et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: TMAO is metabolized by Tat-dependent periplasmic enzymes.
source: Second, we measured growth rates with the anaerobic electron acceptor trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), which is metabolized by Tat-dependent periplasmic enzymes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Amino acid substitutions which prevent translocase assembly should also block transport.
source: Because amino acid substitutions which prevent translocase assembly should also block transport we examined the Tat transport activity of variants at these target salt bridges.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between assembly and transport.

claim: D31K TatA exhibited a low level of Tat transport activity in the SDS assay.
source: When these various salt bridge variants were assessed using the SDS growth assay, which can detect very low levels of Tat activity, transport was now observed for D31K-substituted Tat, although at lower levels than with the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.
